strengths: The paper studies a timely and relevant question: whether Mamba-style state space models are useful as speech self-supervised HuBERT backbones, especially for causal, streaming, and long-context speech settings.
The empirical scope is broader than many prior Mamba-for-speech papers, covering ASR fine-tuning, efficiency measurements, representation analyses, and a MiniSUPERB-style probing suite.

The strongest evidence is in causal and long-context settings: Mamba-based HuBERT shows lower long-sequence compute/RTF trends, avoids OOM where the Transformer baseline fails, improves document-level ASR for ExtBiMamba, and outperforms a causal Transformer on causal ASR with fewer parameters.

The paper is fairly candid about mixed results: bidirectional base-size ExtBiMamba substantially underperforms Transformer HuBERT on SUPERB probing, and the authors identify scalability/design limitations rather than presenting uniformly positive claims.
The phone-purity and CCA analyses provide useful diagnostic evidence beyond downstream scores, and the ablation between ExtBiMamba and InnBiMamba is informative.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is a major concern. Key experimental details are missing or underspecified, including the pretraining corpus, exact data hours, optimizer and learning-rate schedules, masking setup, hardware/training time, random seeds, downstream fine-tuning hyperparameters, and whether code/checkpoints will be released.

Several central claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper calls the study comprehensive, but evaluates only four SUPERB tasks, omits many standard speech SSL comparisons, and does not compare against efficient Transformer/Conformer/streaming baselines or chunked/document ASR alternatives.

The long-context ASR result is promising but not fully controlled. The Transformer baseline is reported as OOM, but there is no comparison to memory-efficient attention, chunking, gradient checkpointing, hierarchical decoding, or other practical long-context baselines. Thus the result supports an efficiency advantage, but less clearly a modeling advantage.

The ASR sections lack sufficient dataset and protocol detail. TEDLIUM3 is specified for long-context ASR, but the causal ASR setup is unclear, and the treatment of talks longer than 20 minutes, segmentation, decoding, language model use, and statistical test units is not detailed enough.

The methodology for representation analysis is under-described. CCA setup, sample sizes, dimensionality handling, normalization, phoneme alignments, and mutual-information computation are not sufficiently specified, making it hard to assess robustness.

The paper sometimes mixes normalized efficiency claims with raw deployment implications. Reporting MACs per second makes Mamba appear nearly constant with sequence length, but RTF still increases; memory usage and latency profiles would be needed for stronger deployment claims.

The empirical picture is uneven: base-size bidirectional Mamba performs much worse than Transformer on SUPERB, and the best bidirectional Mamba variant remains far below Transformer base in overall score. This limits the main-conference case unless the contribution is framed more narrowly around causal/long-context use.

Presentation has some rough edges, including typos, inconsistent terminology such as SUPERB/SUPERBS, and occasional unclear phrasing. These do not undermine the work alone, but they reinforce the need for revision.

strengths: The paper studies a relevant and timely question for speech SSL: whether Mamba-style sequence models can serve as efficient alternatives to Transformer HuBERT models, especially for causal and long-context settings.

The empirical scope is broader than many single-task Mamba speech papers, covering efficiency measurements, ASR fine-tuning, phone-purity analysis, CCA-style representation probes, SUPERB-style probing, and an ablation over bidirectional Mamba variants.

The causal-setting results are potentially useful: Mamba appears competitive or better than a causal Transformer baseline on PR/SID and causal ASR while using fewer parameters, which supports the general direction of the work.

The long-context ASR experiment highlights a practical advantage of linear-time models: document-level processing is feasible for ExtBiMamba where the same-size Transformer baseline runs out of memory.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is a major weakness. The paper omits many essential experimental details: pretraining corpus, exact model configurations, optimizer and schedule, masking settings, k-means target construction details, batch/audio duration, fine-tuning hyperparameters, decoding setup, SUPERB protocol details, random seeds, code/model release status, and sample sizes for statistical tests.

Several central claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper claims streaming ASR advantages, but the experiment appears to be causal ASR rather than a full streaming setup with latency, chunking, endpointing, or online decoding evaluation.

The long-context ASR evidence is narrow: only TEDLIUM3 is used, the comparison is mainly against an OOM Transformer baseline, and no memory-efficient Transformer, chunked Transformer, Conformer, recurrent/SSM baseline, or strong long-context ASR system is included. Thus the result supports feasibility more than superior ASR modeling.

The paper’s strongest positive results are limited to causal settings, while the base-size bidirectional ExtBiMamba substantially underperforms Transformer on all SUPERB metrics. This undercuts the broader claim that Mamba-based HuBERT is a generally strong speech foundation model.

The methodological rigor of the representation analyses is limited. Phone purity and CCA trends are interesting but are not tied convincingly to downstream utility; the claim about better quantized representations for spoken language modeling is not validated with a spoken LM or generation task.

The CCA analysis with speaker and emotion embeddings is under-specified and difficult to interpret, since the “labels” are themselves model-derived embeddings. Without controls, confidence intervals, dataset descriptions, and robustness checks, conclusions about what features are captured more distinctly remain weak.

The SUPERB evaluation is partial, using only four tasks, and results are reported without variance across seeds or runs. Some differences are small, while the paper draws broad conclusions about overall representation quality.

Baselines are not always well matched or fully justified. Mamba and Transformer variants differ in parameter count and architectural components such as the optional MLP, and the paper does not disentangle architecture effects from capacity or training instability.

The efficiency section largely verifies an expected complexity property rather than establishing a new modeling contribution, and the plots lack sufficient numerical detail for independent comparison.

The manuscript has clarity and polish issues, including missing or sparse experimental descriptions, typographical errors such as “probling,” awkward phrasing, and incomplete-looking reference extraction/formatting, which further reduces confidence in readiness.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant question for speech SSL: whether Mamba can serve as a practical alternative to Transformer HuBERT backbones, especially for causal and long-context settings where attention has unfavorable scaling.

The empirical scope is broader than many prior Mamba-in-speech studies: it includes efficiency scaling, long-context ASR, causal ASR, SUPERB-style probing, phone-purity analysis, CCA-based representational analysis, and bidirectional-architecture ablations.

The main positive results are credible and useful: Mamba shows clear computational advantages on long sequences, enables document-level ASR where the comparable Transformer runs out of memory, and outperforms causal Transformer baselines in ASR and several probing settings.

The paper is appropriately nuanced in several places, acknowledging that bidirectional base-scale ExtBiMamba underperforms the Transformer and that Mamba’s bidirectional scalability remains challenging.

The comparisons generally use matched or clearly reported parameter scales, and the inclusion of Mamba+MLP, ExtBiMamba, InnBiMamba, causal Transformer, and naive causal-mask baselines strengthens the empirical picture.
weaknesses: The contribution is primarily exploratory/empirical rather than a new modeling method, and the strongest claims are setting-dependent: Mamba is compelling for causal and long-context use, but base-scale bidirectional Mamba substantially trails the Transformer on SUPERB probing.

Reproducibility is under-specified. Important details such as the SSL pretraining corpus, exact architecture hyperparameters, optimizer/schedule, masking settings, k-means setup, downstream training recipes, seed variation, and code/model release plans are missing or too sparse for reliable replication.

The long-context ASR evidence is promising but narrow: it appears to rely mainly on TEDLIUM3 with one Transformer OOM comparison. More memory-controlled baselines, chunked/streaming Transformer alternatives, or stronger long-context ASR baselines would make the practical claim more convincing.

Statistical support is limited. A paired t-test is reported for one long-context comparison, but most ASR, SUPERB, phone-purity, and CCA results lack confidence intervals, seed variance, or significance testing.

Some analyses are suggestive rather than decisive. Phone purity and CCA trends are interesting, but the paper sometimes interprets them as representation-quality evidence without fully validating their relationship to downstream behavior, especially where phone purity and PR results disagree.

Presentation has several polish issues, including typos such as 'probling', awkward phrasing, and figures whose axes/values are difficult to read. These do not undermine the work, but they reduce clarity.

The efficiency analysis reports MACs/sec and RTF, but the setup needs clearer explanation of batching, implementation kernels, memory accounting, and whether all models are equally optimized; otherwise the exact magnitude of efficiency gains is hard to assess.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely question for speech SSL: whether Mamba-style state space models are a viable alternative to Transformer HuBERT backbones, especially for causal and long-context settings.

The empirical scope is broader than much prior Mamba-in-speech work: the paper studies pretraining, ASR fine-tuning, causal vs bidirectional variants, representation analyses, SUPERB probing, and a full SUPERB appendix for representative models.

The main causal-setting evidence is reasonably convincing: Mamba-based HuBERT improves over a causal Transformer baseline on ASR WER and several SUPERB/probing metrics while using fewer or comparable parameters.

The efficiency analysis supports the expected linear-scaling advantage and is directly tied to an applied use case, long-context ASR, where the Transformer baseline runs out of memory under the authors' setup.

The paper is candid about important limitations, including single-GPU pretraining, smaller batch sizes than original HuBERT, single-run results, and weaker scalability in bidirectional base-size models.
weaknesses: The contribution is mainly an empirical exploration rather than a new method, and several headline claims are only moderately supported. In particular, the long-context ASR result compares ExtBiMamba document-level decoding against a Transformer that OOMs under the authors' budget, but does not compare against memory-optimized attention, chunked/document-aware Transformer baselines, Conformer/Emformer-style streaming baselines, or other long-context ASR methods.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says the codebase is available but the URL is blank, and many implementation details needed to reproduce pretraining and fine-tuning exactly are not fully specified, including batch construction, hardware-dependent memory settings, downstream heads, decoding details, and statistical testing protocol.

The experimental evidence relies on single training runs, with no variance estimates or repeated seeds for expensive but central comparisons. This weakens confidence because the reported gains on some tasks are modest and Mamba training stability is itself identified as an issue.

The baselines are fair in some respects but still limited. The paper retrains Transformer HuBERT under the same constrained single-GPU setup, but this setting is substantially weaker than standard HuBERT training, so the conclusions may reflect this constrained regime rather than general architectural superiority.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence. For example, higher phone purity is framed as producing higher-quality quantized representations, but the paper itself shows that this does not consistently translate to PR probing performance, and the causal/bidirectional results are mixed across tasks.

The bidirectional results reduce the broader impact of the work: base-size ExtBiMamba underperforms Transformer across all reported SUPERB metrics, and the stronger InnBiMamba ablation still remains below the Transformer base overall, suggesting the method is not a general replacement for Transformer-based speech SSL.

Presentation is generally understandable but has polish issues: some equations/text have formatting artifacts, figure/table readability is uneven in extraction, and the missing code link is a conspicuous omission for a reproducibility-oriented paper.

strengths: The paper studies a relevant question for speech SSL: whether Mamba-style sequence models can serve as HuBERT backbones, especially for causal and long-context speech settings where Transformer attention is costly.
The experimental scope is broader than a single downstream task, covering ASR fine-tuning, efficiency measurements, representation analyses, four SUPERB probing tasks, and a fuller SUPERB appendix.
The causal-setting results are the most convincing part: Mamba variants outperform causal Transformer baselines on PR/SID and overall SUPERB-style scores, while using fewer or comparable parameters.
The paper is transparent about some limitations, including single-run reporting, reduced batch size relative to original HuBERT, and instability/scaling issues for bidirectional Mamba models.
weaknesses: The main claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper repeatedly frames Mamba-based HuBERT as broadly promising, but the bidirectional Base model substantially underperforms the Transformer on probing and full SUPERB results, and utterance-level ASR is worse than the Transformer baseline.

The long-context ASR evidence is too narrow to support strong conclusions. The Transformer baseline is reported as OOM at document level, but the paper does not compare against practical long-context Transformer alternatives such as chunking, memory-efficient attention, segment recurrence, hierarchical inference, or optimized attention kernels.

Reproducibility is weak: the abstract says the codebase is available, but the URL is blank in the manuscript. Results are from a single run, and important implementation details for pretraining, fine-tuning, MAC/RTF measurement, clustering, and CCA are insufficient for faithful reproduction.

The methodology raises fairness concerns. Models differ in parameter count, use different learning rates, and are trained under a single-GPU regime that is known to underperform standard HuBERT; this makes it hard to separate architectural effects from training-budget and optimization effects.

The evaluation is selective in the main text. The primary SUPERB comparison uses only four tasks, while the full appendix shows a more mixed picture, including clear Transformer superiority in the bidirectional setting.

The representational analyses are suggestive but not rigorously tied to downstream behavior. Phone purity and CCA trends are interpreted strongly, yet the paper itself notes that higher purity does not align with PR probing, weakening the causal explanatory claims.

The streaming/causal ASR framing is underdeveloped. Reporting no-lookahead causal WER is useful, but there is no full streaming evaluation with latency, online decoding constraints, endpointing, or comparison to established streaming ASR systems.
Presentation quality has issues, including missing code link, occasional formatting/spacing problems, and some imprecise or speculative wording. These reduce confidence in polish and reproducibility.

strengths: Timely and relevant empirical study of Mamba-based HuBERT for speech self-supervised learning, covering causal, bidirectional, long-context ASR, streaming/causal ASR, SUPERB probing, and representation analyses rather than a single isolated downstream task.

The central efficiency claim is well motivated and supported by sequence-length experiments showing favorable scaling of Mamba models, with practical implications for long-context speech processing where Transformer baselines run out of memory under the authors' setup.

The causal-setting results are convincing and useful: Mamba-based HuBERT improves over causal Transformer baselines on ASR WER and several SUPERB-style metrics while using fewer or comparable parameters.

The paper is refreshingly balanced in places: it reports failures and limitations for bidirectional/base-scale Mamba, includes ablations over ExtBiMamba vs. InnBiMamba, and discusses training instability rather than hiding it.

Representation analyses using phone purity and CCA add interpretability beyond benchmark numbers and support the claim that Mamba and Transformer architectures encode some speech attributes differently.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is only partial. The abstract says the codebase is available but the link is missing in the extracted manuscript, and several implementation details needed to reproduce the pretraining/fine-tuning pipeline, exact batching, hardware memory settings, and SUPERB setup are not fully specified.

Most reported results appear to come from a single pretraining/fine-tuning run. Given the known instability of Mamba variants and the relatively modest performance gaps in some comparisons, lack of variance estimates or repeated runs limits confidence in fine-grained conclusions.

The long-context ASR comparison is useful but not fully conclusive: the Transformer baseline is reported as OOM, but there is no comparison to memory-efficient attention, chunked attention, FlashAttention-style implementations, hierarchical/segmented baselines, or other practical long-context ASR systems. This weakens the breadth of the claim that Mamba is the better long-context alternative.

The experimental scale is constrained to single-GPU pretraining with smaller effective batch size than original HuBERT, and the authors acknowledge that their Transformer baseline underperforms official released models. This makes the study sound as a controlled comparison but limits claims about competitiveness at modern SSL scale.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence warrants. For example, 'higher-quality quantized representations' is mostly supported by phone purity, yet downstream PR does not always improve, and the paper itself notes that purity does not guarantee discriminability.

The bidirectional results are mixed: base-scale ExtBiMamba substantially underperforms Transformer on SUPERB and full SUPERB, so the contribution is strongest for causal/streaming and efficiency settings rather than as a general replacement for Transformer-based speech SSL.

Presentation has minor polish issues, including formatting glitches in equations/tables, missing code URL, and occasional imprecise wording around streaming ASR despite experiments being causal/no-lookahead rather than a full deployed streaming evaluation with latency constraints.
